accuracy.evidence: Checked against Cepeda et al. (2006) meta-analysis of distributed practice (spaced beats massed for equal study time), Cepeda et al. (2008) on optimal gaps growing with the retention interval, Dunlosky et al. (2013) rating distributed practice high utility, and Ebbinghaus (1885) for the forgetting curve. The lab's model R = e^(-t/S), with S multiplied by 1 + 2.5(1 - R) at each review, is labelled simplified on screen and in the adult text; its outputs (cram days 10-13 keeps 25% at day 30, days 1, 3, 7, 13 keeps 53%; +1, +3, +7 best of all six orders at 39%) were computed and checked by script.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips: fluency illusion that cramming works (plan step shows crammed test day high but day 30 at 25%, Why does cramming feel like it works challenge), reviewing straight away (Day 0: still 100% recalled. Too soon), waiting until it is gone (Too late: you would be relearning it), fixed equal gaps (expanding-schedule step and Day 1, 2, 3 distractor), and re-reading in a row taken as spacing (sort step, reread challenge).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagspaced is a live forgetting-curve simulator: a 13-day calendar of toggles drives a recall chart to day 30 with test-day and day-30 readouts, a tap-the-chart review timing task whose good window moves later each round (S = 2, 5, 10 days), and a three-slot gap builder that redraws the curve for each order. It differs from flagrecall (Testing yourself: retrieval practice) and flagmem (How memory works); gate_lab_distinct passes on 6-token shingles.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers the spacing effect by experiment before it is named in the done message: placing four days and reading the day-30 value, then seeing a crammed plan fail with its own numbers. Review timing gives exact recall percentages for too soon and too late; a wrong gap order is redrawn and explained (Waiting 7 days first lets the new memory fade too far) before resetting. Show me completes every task on iPhone 13 and desktop.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions, each tested by the step that follows: same four sessions crammed vs spread for day 30; best review time straight after vs when getting hard to recall; best gaps short-then-long vs long-then-short. The wrong options are the intuitive answers named in the adult misconceptions paragraph, and the done message reports the learner's own prediction.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six fresh challenge items (Lena's 3 hours of French, first review timing, which schedule is expanding, why cramming feels like it works, which is spaced, how gaps should change) with answer order rotated. Each wrong option has its own why() line, for example 1 hour on each of the last 3 days gets Those are bunched at the end: still crammed, and Day 7, 10, 11 gets Those gaps shrink (7, 3, 1).

readability.evidence: Learner audience: kid explanation FK 4.6 (limit 7.0), adult FK 8.2 (limit 10.0). Terms defined in plain words where they appear: forgetting curve, cramming and massed practice, spaced or distributed practice, spacing effect, expanding schedule. On-canvas prompts are single sentences, and chart labels are percentages and day numbers an 11-year-old reads easily.

no_filler.evidence: Each paragraph carries one idea with a concrete case: the curve, cram vs spread at equal time, review timing with too soon and too late, growing gaps of 1, 3 and 7 days and revisiting last month's work. gate_content passes the filler and similarity checks; the family tip is a specific calendar-and-self-quiz routine.

mobile.evidence: Walked on iPhone 13 and desktop 1200x900 in dark and light: the 13 calendar cells fit one row, the chart y-axis labels sit inside the canvas after widening the left margin, gap slots and tiles fit three across, and the sort card and boxes do not overlap. Every canvas action has a button twin (Day 1 to 13 toggles with Clear, Day 0 to 12 review buttons, +1/+3/+7 gap buttons, Spaced/Massed). No console errors.

accessibility.evidence: axe wcag2a, wcag2aa and wcag21aa clean in both themes in the browser gate. speak() updates the canvas aria-label with each result including the numbers (Day 30: 53%. Spreading the same 4 sessions keeps far more a month later), toggles have aria-labels such as Study on day 3 / Remove study on day 3, and challenge feedback is an aria-live status.
